```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

After counting satisfaction, the coordinator asks about assessment scores and
income. `summ()` gives a first look at measurements; `tabstat()` makes a compact
table of means. Both fit into dplyr pipelines and return results you can reuse.

## Start with meaningful measurements

Here are the same twelve participants from
[Getting started](getting-started.html), with income already cleaned and
the two assessment items retained. Income is monthly; scores run from 0 to 10.

```{r survey, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidystata)

survey <- tribble(
  ~id, ~centre,     ~income, ~score1, ~score2,
    1, "Riverside",    1200,       2,       4,
    2, "Riverside",    1500,       4,      NA,
    3, "Riverside",      NA,      NA,      NA,
    4, "Riverside",      NA,       6,       8,
    5, "Riverside",    2200,       8,      10,
    6, "Riverside",    1800,       4,       6,
    7, "Hilltop",      1400,       3,       5,
    8, "Hilltop",      2100,       5,       7,
    9, "Hilltop",      2600,       7,       9,
   10, "Hilltop",        NA,       9,      NA,
   11, "Hilltop",      2300,      NA,       8,
   12, "Hilltop",      1700,       6,       8
)

survey |> summ(income, starts_with("score"))
```

The default columns show observed counts, distinct values, minimum, mean,
sample standard deviation and maximum. The selected measurements have
different observed counts because missingness differs across items.
We leave out `id`: being stored as a number does not make a column a measurement.

## Ask for just the statistics you need

If the question is simply how average scores compare, start with `tabstat()`:

```{r means}
survey |> tabstat(starts_with("score"), .by = centre)
```

It uses the same calculations as `summ()`, but reports only the mean by default.
For a reporting table, choose statistics and their order explicitly:

```{r selected-statistics}
survey |>
  summ(income, .by = centre, .stat = c("n", "mean", "median", "sd"))
```

Missing measured values are omitted from each calculation. `sd` uses the sample
denominator, and undefined statistics are `NA`, for example an SD based on
one observation. Use `.detail = TRUE` to explore the full supported set;
`.stat` takes precedence when you supply it.

For completeness, ask for counts and the observed proportion together:

```{r completeness}
survey |>
  summ(starts_with("score"), .stat = c("n", "miss_n", "valid_pct", "mean"))
```

`miss_n` (also called `missing`) counts missing measurements. `valid_pct`
is a **0-1 proportion**, unlike the 0-100 percentages from `tab()`.

## Calculate first, then summarise

Named expressions can create a column for this summary without changing the
source tibble:

```{r computed}
survey |> summ(income_thousands = income / 1000, .by = centre)
```

For a measurement that you will reuse, create it in `mutate()`. The row average
uses whichever assessment items are observed; it stays missing when neither is.

```{r reusable-score}
scored <- survey |>
  mutate(score = row_mean(pick(score1, score2)))

scored |>
  summ(score, .by = centre, .stat = c("n", "mean", "sd")) |>
  arrange(desc(mean))
```

The centre comparison now uses one score per participant. An explicit `.name =
TRUE` retains a `name` column even when summarising a single variable.

## Make grouping choices explicit

`summ()` and `tabstat()` inherit `group_by()` groups, or accept `.by` for one
operation. Their results are ungrouped. An explicit `.by` replaces inherited
groups. Computed expressions inside `summ()` are evaluated before grouping;
use grouped `mutate()` first for calculations that depend on each group's values.

Suppose participant 12's centre was not recorded. Keep that participant's
measurement visible as a separate group:

```{r missing-centre}
unknown_centre <- scored |>
  mutate(centre = if_else(id == 12, NA_character_, centre))

unknown_centre |> summ(score, .by = centre, .stat = c("n", "mean"))
```

Use `.missing = FALSE` to exclude missing **grouping keys**:

```{r exclude-missing-centre}
unknown_centre |>
  summ(score, .by = centre, .missing = FALSE, .stat = c("n", "mean"))
```

That option does not change how missing measurements are handled.

## Read percentiles using Stata's rule

Percentiles are useful when a mean hides a wide income distribution. Request
`median`, `q1`, `q3`, or percentiles such as `p10` and `p90`:

```{r percentiles}
survey |> summ(income, .stat = c("n", "p10", "q1", "median", "q3", "p90"))
```

These follow Stata's percentile rule, which can differ from R's default
`quantile()`. A small example makes the difference visible:

```{r percentile-rule}
tibble(score = 1:4) |> summ(score, .stat = c("p25", "p50", "p75"))
```

The quartiles are 1.5 and 3.5. For percentile-rank columns, use
`dplyr::percent_rank()`; for quantile groups, use `xtile()`.
`pc()` instead calculates each value's percentage of a total.

## Distinguish frequency and analytic weights

Suppose an aggregate register has three score values and their frequencies.
Frequency weights reproduce the expanded participants:

```{r frequency-weights}
register <- tribble(
  ~score, ~people,
       2,       3,
       6,       1,
      10,       1
)

register |>
  summ(score, .wt = people, .stat = c("n", "mean", "sd", "p50"))
```

The reported `n` is five. Analytic weights rescale to the observed row count
within each variable and group, changing the reported count and sample SD:

```{r analytic-weights}
register |>
  summ(
    score, .wt = people, .wt_type = "analytic",
    .stat = c("n", "mean", "sd")
  )
```

The mean agrees, but `n` is now three. Weights must be finite and nonnegative;
missing weights exclude rows with a message. These are descriptive weighting
rules, not design-based standard errors for a complex survey.

## Choose a convenient return form

Numeric and calendar variables have different units, so the default separates
their summaries into a list when both families occur. Request `.type = "tibble"`
when you need one combined table:

```{r calendar}
visits <- tibble(
  score = c(4, 8),
  day = readr::parse_date(c("2026-09-01", "2026-09-03"))
)

visits |> summ(.type = "tibble", .stat = c("n", "min", "mean", "max"))
```

Shared location columns become character so they can hold numbers and dates.
The default separate tables preserve each family's statistic types. See the
[conventions guide](containers-and-missing-values.html) for calendar spread
units and container preservation.

Unsupported non-numeric columns are omitted with a message. `.keep_all = TRUE`
keeps them for counts and distinct values. Labelled numeric variables use
their codes; factors use level codes and produce a message. Select meaningful
measurements instead of averaging category codes. Entirely missing columns
still warn and remain with `n = 0` and `NA` statistics, including `sum`;
`.drop_empty = TRUE` omits those rows.

## Look at relationships next

Do income and the two assessment items move together? `corr()` uses one common
complete sample across all selected columns:

```{r correlation}
survey |> corr(income, score1, score2)
```

`pwcorr()` instead uses the available observations for each pair, reporting
counts and p-values:

```{r pairwise-correlation}
survey |> pwcorr(income, score1, score2)
```

Compare the `n` columns: changing the missing-data rule changes which participants
contribute. `pwcorr(.listwise = TRUE)` uses a common sample. `spearman()` computes
rank correlations on a common sample by default, with `.pairwise = TRUE` for
pairwise samples. The tiny survey illustrates the interfaces, not evidence
about programme effects. See the [correlation reference](https://socimh.github.io/tidystata/reference/corr.html)
for additional options.

Return to [data preparation](inspect-and-prepare.html) to build measurements,
or use [category tables](tabulation.html) for responses that are categories.
